**Why Team Fortress 2 is One of the Greatest Games of All Time**

*Team Fortress 2* (TF2), developed by Valve and released in 2007, has earned its place as one of the greatest multiplayer first-person shooters of all time. With its unique art style, balanced class-based gameplay, and strong community support, TF2 has remained relevant for nearly two decades. Despite the emergence of countless modern shooters, TF2’s charm, depth, and fun factor make it a timeless classic.

### **Unique Art Style and Personality**
One of TF2’s most recognizable features is its distinct visual style. Unlike many shooters that strive for hyper-realistic graphics, TF2 embraces a cartoonish, exaggerated aesthetic reminiscent of classic animated films. This choice not only gives the game a unique identity but also ensures that it ages well. The vibrant character designs and fluid animations make the game visually appealing and easy to follow, even in chaotic battles.

Additionally, TF2’s personality shines through in its cast of nine diverse characters. Each class has a well-defined persona, complete with unique voice lines, animations, and backstories. The humor and charm embedded in their interactions make TF2 not just a game but an experience filled with character and wit.

### **Deep and Balanced Gameplay**
TF2’s class-based system sets it apart from other first-person shooters. With nine distinct classes—Scout, Soldier, Pyro, Demoman, Heavy, Engineer, Medic, Sniper, and Spy—the game offers a playstyle for everyone. Each class serves a unique role, creating a dynamic team-based experience where cooperation is key to victory.

Unlike many modern shooters that rely heavily on aim mechanics alone, TF2 emphasizes strategy and teamwork. A well-coordinated team of diverse classes will always outperform a group of players who simply chase kills. This emphasis on balance and role fulfillment creates a rewarding gameplay loop that keeps players coming back for more.

### **Constant Evolution and Community Support**
Despite being released over a decade ago, TF2 has managed to stay relevant thanks to continuous updates, new content, and a passionate community. Over the years, Valve has introduced new weapons, maps, and game modes, keeping the gameplay fresh. The introduction of the Mann-Conomy update, which added a cosmetic and trading system, further deepened player engagement.

Additionally, the TF2 community plays a significant role in the game’s longevity. Modders and content creators have developed custom maps, weapons, and game modes that continue to breathe life into the game. Community-run servers and events help sustain an active player base, even in the absence of frequent official updates.

### **A Perfect Blend of Casual and Competitive Play**
Another reason for TF2’s greatness is its ability to cater to both casual and competitive players. For those who want a lighthearted, fun experience, TF2 offers a variety of game modes such as Payload, King of the Hill, and Capture the Flag. The game’s humor, combined with wacky mechanics like rocket jumping and taunts, ensures that even casual matches feel entertaining.

On the other hand, TF2 also provides a rewarding competitive experience. Skilled players can master movement mechanics, team strategies, and advanced techniques to dominate the battlefield. The balance between accessible fun and high-skill potential makes TF2 a game that welcomes newcomers while also challenging veterans.

### **A Legacy That Endures**
Few games can claim to have the same lasting impact as *Team Fortress 2*. Its unique aesthetic, well-balanced gameplay, and strong community have allowed it to thrive despite the ever-changing gaming landscape. While many games fade into obscurity, TF2 continues to be a beloved title that attracts both old and new players.

In a world where live-service shooters rise and fall, TF2 remains a shining example of how great design, personality, and player-driven content can create a game that stands the test of time. Whether you’re a longtime fan or a newcomer, TF2’s greatness is undeniable—and it’s always a good time to jump into the action.

After playing this game on and off for over a decade (even though the playtime wouldn’t really suggest it), I have come to the conclusion that this game should be taken off life support, something Valve would obviously celebrate, as evidenced by complete disregard of the player base time and time again.

Team Fortress 2 is so, so painfully a product of its time, where “its time” is every single time Valve pushed out a large update. We got cosmetics (also limited-time ones, given for arbitrary reasons) and microtransactions, then matchmaking and some perverse version of achievements with rewards (Jungle Inferno contracts, anyone?) Finally, we settled on rampant cheating. If I could, I would instead write a review on Valve Anti-Cheat, but here we are…

Botting on TF2 got so bad that it was impossible to play, which is something that Valve doesn’t care about anymore if there’s profit in there somewhere. It was only after the community rallied together that Valve “fixed” the issue, but, to this day, if you play long enough and pay enough attention, you will run into more “subtle” cheaters every few games, because commercial solutions exist to cater to such audiences (see: LMAOBOX). Valve’s “anti-cheat” can be completely bypassed by existing open-source code snippets, leading us back to the point that TF2 is truly a product of its time, where basic detection techniques were good enough and everything else past that was duct-taped on top. Now, with the game being maintained by a skeleton crew, there is simply no hope of the situation ever improving. There might be further instances of grand ban waves, but, in the end, it's a war of attrition that Valve will lose.

Taking a small detour on to other things stemming from the game’s age - if you’ve played Quake about as long as TF2, you’ll be experiencing a familiar aura of “the meta must not be broken” throughout several game modes (“ye intel shalt not be capped” in CTF and “thou shalt not suck” in Mann Up), not to mention getting destroyed by players with thousands upon thousands of hours spent playing, who may or may not be cheating. Despite all that, there are always new players to be found. Bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, they try to have fun in whatever way they see fit, but the more grizzled veterans know that having newbies in your team means getting stomped in a match.

“Why?”, you ask, “doesn’t the matchmaking system use some sort of rating to balance things out? Aren’t teams rebalanced if someone leaves or joins?”

*sigh*

after only taking a short 4 years to fix the chronic botting problem, valve has finally made the real tf2 casual experience accessible: experiencing someone being racist every 3 games because valve's approach to moderation is 'moderation is for losers who do treadmill work'
if that doesn't appeal to you, feel free to join one of three popular community server networks to play a grand total of eight of the 100+ maps in the game because people can't imagine playing something other than the grand sniper sightline that is upward

[i]but if you can just ignore all that[/i]
The actual gameplay of TF2 is great, another testament to the raw talent that works at Valve, even nearly 20 years later (and some 8 years after the last time they felt like putting effort into a TF2 update). Nine classes with unique gameplay, greatly written characters, and a timeless artstyle. MvM is a great PvE mode, and the community server browser holds countless alternate gamemodes should the standard PvP get boring.
The game does still regularly receive seasonal updates consisting of community-made content, but by this point, the party was basically over some ten years ago. The game will continue to have some solid gameplay into the future (barring another 'bot crisis' or some other 'I can't play the game anymore' event), but it's unlikely TF2 will ever reach the heights of its heyday again.

"Team Fortress 2" is a timeless multiplayer game that has managed to stay relevant for years despite being released in 2007. Its unique blend of humor, class-based gameplay, and strategic depth has created a dedicated community that still enjoys the game today. The colorful, cartoony art style and witty writing make it stand out in a sea of more serious first-person shooters. Every character feels distinct, with each class bringing something different to the table. Whether you prefer the heavy firepower of the Heavy, the tactical precision of the Engineer, or the speed and agility of the Scout, there’s a playstyle for everyone.

What sets "Team Fortress 2" apart from other shooters is the teamwork aspect. Each class is designed to complement the others, meaning successful teams need coordination and communication. It's not just about getting the most kills; it's about supporting your teammates, setting up defenses, or pushing forward as a group. The game rewards team-based strategies and encourages players to think about the bigger picture, rather than going solo.

The game's balance between casual fun and competitive depth is another key element. While it’s easy to jump into a match and enjoy yourself, there’s also room for serious players to refine their skills and master each class. The constantly evolving updates, new weapons, and maps help keep the experience fresh, with each update adding new content or gameplay adjustments to keep things interesting.

One of the most enjoyable aspects of "Team Fortress 2" is its community. The game has a rich history of fan-created content, from custom maps to user-made skins and mods. The game’s accessibility and open nature have allowed it to grow into something much bigger than just a simple shooter. Despite its age, "Team Fortress 2" continues to be an enjoyable and engaging game, filled with quirky moments and memorable experiences that keep players coming back time and time again.

185411723.review:
To new players who may have only played games like hero shooters, or battle royales, extraction shooters: 

I recommend giving TF2 an earnest try! It's a different flavor of shooter with a few game modes, like capture the flag, king of the hill, payload (which is used in Overwatch and Marvel Rivals), and capture points. There's a lot more, but those are the main ones played by the casual community. There's a niche for everyone, even for people who don't have much aiming proficiency. 

There's a lot of depth to the game to the point that you may find this game to be the perfect launching point if you want to get good at shooting games in general. And for those who want to get serious, there's a community competitive scene as well who plays mainly 6v6 capture point gamemodes. It's probably easier to get into these leagues than most private leagues for other games, because there are lots of beginners. There are also a lot of easy to access community servers that are great resources for practice, like "MGE" servers, and rocket jump maps which helps make it easy to learn more in-depth mechanics.

The gunplay in this game is unique because every weapon has a bit physics, a bit of push and pull to it. This means that if you get hit by an explosive rather than just having to sit there and take it, you can jump and "surf" the the explosion and strafing in mid air to position yourself better and dodge further damage. It's the same with almost every weapon. This style of gameplay helps to make the game feel fair in almost every interaction with other players, which you may find to be rare in a lot of other games where you just have to accept what's happening. That also means the skill ceiling is insanely high. 

The netcoding is also very responsive in this game. You have a degree of player control to use the net settings that most suit your environment, and I find this system makes the game way more responsive than any other shooter out there. This is a game where you can see where the opponent is aiming, and actively dodge their point of aim. That is, unless the ping difference is too high. That said, in other games you may never experience that even at the best case scenario, often being defeated by opponents that never seemed to be looking at you. 

This game still has a huge player base and you'll quickly find a casual game every time. Casual is truly casual, you don't have to think about a single thing. The games are 12v12, so there's less of an individual responsibility. Yet if you become quite good at the game, you will find that you can have a huge impact even in a 24 player server. 

No one has ever tried to make a copy of TF2, exactly the way that it is, and I think that's a testimony to how well they did it. 👍👍

The F-22 Raptor is a fifth-generation, single-seat, twin-engine stealth tactical fighter aircraft developed for the United States Air Force (USAF). Designed primarily as an air superiority fighter, the F-22 integrates advanced stealth, supercruise capability, maneuverability, and situational awareness to dominate in air-to-air and air-to-ground missions.

Design and Specifications
Dimensions:
Length: 62 feet (18.9 meters)
Wingspan: 44.5 feet (13.6 meters)
Height: 16.7 feet (5.08 meters)
Wing Area: 840 square feet (78.0 square meters)

Weight:
Empty Weight: Approximately 43,340 pounds (19,700 kg)
Maximum Takeoff Weight: About 83,500 pounds (37,500 kg)

Engines:
Type: Two Pratt & Whitney F119-PW-100 turbofan engines
Thrust: Each engine produces 35,000 pounds of thrust, with afterburner thrust exceeding 50,000 pounds, enabling supercruise (sustained supersonic flight without afterburners).

Performance:
Maximum Speed: Over Mach 2.0 (approximately 1,500 mph or 2,414 km/h)
Combat Range: Around 1,839 miles (2,960 km) without refueling
Service Ceiling: 65,000 feet (19,812 meters)

Stealth and Avionics
Stealth Features: The F-22 employs advanced stealth technology to reduce its radar cross-section (RCS) significantly. This includes its unique shape, radar-absorbent materials, and internal weapons bays that minimize exposure to enemy radar.
Avionics: It is equipped with a highly integrated avionics suite, including a sophisticated radar system (AN/APG-77) that features low probability of intercept and can track multiple targets simultaneously. The F-22 also uses advanced sensors and data fusion capabilities to provide pilots with unparalleled situational awareness.
Armament
The F-22 Raptor is designed to carry a mix of air-to-air and air-to-ground munitions, including:

Air-to-Air Missiles:
AIM-120 AMRAAM (Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile)
AIM-9 Sidewinder (short-range infrared missile)

Air-to-Ground Munitions:
GBU-32 JDAM (Joint Direct Attack Munition)
GBU-39 Small Diameter Bomb (SDB)

The aircraft has an internal weapons bay that can carry up to 2,000 pounds of munitions, as well as two underwing hardpoints for additional ordnance.

Role and Capabilities
Air Superiority: The F-22 excels in establishing air dominance, capable of engaging enemy aircraft at long ranges while maintaining a low radar profile.
Multirole Operations: While primarily an air-to-air fighter, the F-22 can also perform air-to-ground strikes, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare missions.
Network-Centric Warfare: The F-22 is designed for operation in a network-centric environment, enabling it to share information with other friendly forces and command systems seamlessly.

Operational History
The F-22 entered service with the USAF in 2005 and has since been deployed in various operations, including air patrols, training exercises, and international deployments.
It remains a critical component of the USAF's air power, maintaining a technological edge over potential adversaries.

It is impossible to explain just how much of an impact this game has had on me ever since I started playing it. It is probably one of the best multiplayer games you can experience, even after ~17 years.
Which is why it is so painful to see the state it is in.

It is very evident in Valve's actions (or lack thereof) that they do not care about this game unless it loses them money. No content has been added in the last ~7 years that hasn't been community made content that they are, frankly, too lazy to make themselves. Why waste effort and resources on updating the game when we have people that will do it for us?
Part of this "content" is lootboxes, or "Community Crates," a predatory way to take people's money, using hats, cosmetics, and particle effects (which they didn't make) that, while thankfully not giving an advantage against other players, contribute to a system where Valve is able to make money without actually caring for the game and giving its players anything meaningful in return.

Of course, every few years or so, a wave of bots swarm official servers with the intention of ruining the game for others, which consists of headshotting everyone as Sniper and spamming slurs in chat. They are gone (for now) as I am writing this, but I am not going to say that they are gone for good.
Along the way, of course, are Valve's actions regarding getting rid of the bots. One of these "fixes" include disabling chat for F2P players, due to the "spamming slurs" thing, which:
1. Straight up did not work, bot spam proceeded as usual.
2. Gimped genuine new players unless they spent money in the *official* store.
3. Showed the incompetence of Valve and turned the community against them even harder.

It is simply impossible for me to recommend this game to someone in its current state. It is so disappointing to see this amount of corporate greed and incompetence from "small indie game company" Valve.
I urge anyone reading this to not buy anything through the in-game store or Steam Marketplace, especially the seasonal crates, as it shows Valve that we are "happy" with the state the game is in.

176185586.review:
Team Fortress 2 is one of my favorite games and hat simulators of all time. It's not really much of a secret, given how many hours I've gotten in it plus the fact I've been playing it for over 10 years (although it was a while before I had a computer that could run it very well). It is more than just a game; it is a whole experience.

The gameplay is very addictive. The gunplay and counters feel just right, and no two classes play the same (which can't be said for some modern hero shooters). Team Fortress 2 showed that you only needed 9 classes maximum, instead of 20 or so. There are crates and microtransactions sure, but they aren't exactly forced upon you; you can simply get free item drops by just playing the game on servers (at least if they are secure VAC-enabled ones). A lot of the maps are very memorable; 2Fort, Dustbowl, Badwater etc. and a dozen of community created maps that would be too much to list here. Even with (non-cheating) singleplayer bots, the game is still very fun.

Personality and style wise, TF2 had the best a shooter game could ever have. The classes are all fun to witness, and even 17 years later they still feel irreplaceable, with perfect voice acting and beyond memorable and hilarious dialog. It's not like some other games where they are just generic, too. Each class was designed with shapes and silhouettes in mind, creating easily identifiable looks (i.e. if someone is outlined behind a wall, you could tell which class it is even from afar). The art-style of the game, inspired by J.C. Leyendecker, really made it timeless, and it still looks good to this day; an incredible feat for a game from 2007, a time when most games went for a muddy realistic look (a large portion of which haven't aged well visually). TF2 went for a heavily researched mixture of being cartoony and grounded, and it worked very, VERY well. It's not like some modern cartoony shooters that don't have reason behind the style, because this one does. There is also a story that is not forced upon you, being told through item descriptions, map objects, comics and shorts. It is wacky and adds a lot more to the game's world.

Now sure, the game has had its rough times. The Meet Your Match update was an attempt at making TF2 appeal to the e-sports scene, when really it was a game that you could pick up and just... play (hence why Quickplay was a thing). There was (currently remedied) also the botting crisis that lead to all sorts of different things (drama, campaigns, review bombings etc.). None of these affect my opinion on the game itself, however. You don't HAVE to play on Casual and Competitive; you can make your own server or join community ones. I only have minor criticisms with some weapon balancing decisions and bugs, but they aren't enough to lower my thoughts on the game. I do also wish that the classes had more unique lines for interacting with each other, rather than them being stuck to domination lines (think Left 4 Dead 2 or even Overwatch, where characters would refer to each other by name and talk if nearby).

I feel this review was long, long overdue (10 years overdue, even). I never really made serious reviews until now, but I figured I'd finally do so. Team Fortress 2 is not only one of the most important shooters, but also one of the most important games alone to me. It's a game that will never die to me, because even if the official servers shut off, you can still host your own and get others to join or play with singleplayer bots. Even playing with stock weapons is still fun. I'll probably still be playing in a decade or more from now. It just never gets old, even 17 years later.

[h3][b][u]Team Fortress 2[/u][/b][/h3] is a team-based first-person shooter developed by Valve Corporation. Released in 2007, it has become a cult classic and remains one of the most popular PC games of all time. Here's a breakdown of what makes TF2 so special:

[b][u]Unique Classes:[/u][/b] TF2 features nine distinct classes, each with its own strengths, weaknesses, and playstyle. The classes are divided into three categories: Offense (Scout, Soldier, Pyro), Defence (Demo-man, Heavy, Engineer), and Support (Medic, Sniper, Spy). Each class has a set of unique abilities, which encourages players to work together as a team and use their skills to overcome opponents.

[b][u]Game Play:[/u][/b] The game play in TF2 is incredibly polished, with tight controls and responsive movement. Players can choose from various game modes, including Capture the Flag, Control Point, and Payload. The objective-based game play and diverse classes ensure that no two matches are ever the same.

[b][u]Visuals and Soundtrack:[/u][/b] TF2's cartoon-ish, stylised visuals have become iconic in the world of gaming. The game's art style, inspired by the works of J.J. Sedelmaier and Chuck Jones, has aged surprisingly well, and the character designs are instantly recognisable. The soundtrack, composed by Mike Morasky and John Patrick Lowrie, is equally impressive, with catchy and humorous theme songs for each class.

[b][u]Community:[/u][/b] The TF2 community is dedicated and passionate, with a strong focus on competitive play and teamwork. While the community can be toxic at times, Valve has implemented various measures to reduce harassment and promote positive behaviour. The game's popularity has also led to the creation of numerous community-made maps, game modes, and cosmetics.

[b][u]Influence:[/u][/b] TF2's influence can be seen in many modern shooters, including Overwatch, Rainbow Six Siege, and Team Fortress's own spiritual successor, Overwatch's Payload mode. The game's innovative game play mechanics, such as the " ubercharge" system and the emphasis on teamwork, have become staples of the genre.

[b][u]Price:[/u][/b] The best part? Team Fortress 2 is completely free to play, with no upfront cost or subscription fees. Players can purchase in-game items and cosmetics, but the core game play experience is entirely free.

[i]Overall, Team Fortress 2 is a game that has stood the test of time, and its unique blend of game play, humour, and style continues to captivate audiences to this day. If you haven't already, do yourself a favour and give it a try – you won't regret it.[/i]

I'm not gonna blurb the whole history, but basically 7 years ago they removed a bunch of skill ceilings, ruining lots of guns and playstyles making previous sidegrades straight up or downgrades. Pyro got a bunch of nonsense which they've helped a little with (flame hitbox was mad broken). Then the updates stopped, and 4 years later or even sooner it was a bot infested hellscape you couldn't hope to play on official servers. They've done ban waves now so in that aspect it's playable again. Matchmaking hasn't been touched since release though so hope you don't mind putting 200hrs in to get the basics and researching playstyles/mechanics. 
   Even with all that there's lots to enjoy here. A shooter where firefights are more than a milisecond, unique playstyles, gamemodes, and communites. It's a game where you experience is what you make of it, like movement shooters? Play an explosives, scout, hell wrangler engie. More of a point and click? Sniper and spy will have you covered. Want a hero shooter less based in moba mechanics? Here you are. All the weapons are free, and for many there's even money to be made (hense bot crisis). If you're going to give it a shot, do your homework first and you'll have a wayy better time. I still probably consider this my favorite game, it's just gotten too disheartening playing in this state. This game introduced me to pc games and I'll always love it deeply, but please don't spend money on it. I need to see valve give more than half a shot to put my heart into it again.

Gameplay is fast-paced, chaotic, and, most importantly, fun. One of [i] TF2’s [/i] greatest strengths is its community. 167665571.review:
Leaving this negative review truly breaks my heart, because I've played this game on and off obsessively since I was 14. Months ago, I told myself I would write a positive, heart-gushing review once I hit 2k hours, but it looks like the odds of me reaching that are getting lower and lower. With the FixTF2 movement seemingly failing, I am just about ready to give up hope here. 

This game has aged fantastically and is somehow able to hold up just as well as modern FPS releases, arguably better than most if I'm being honest. It's been a talked-to-death topic already that I won't drag out here, but the short version is this is a fantastic shooter with the perfect amount of mobility mechanics to feel unique and special with a deceptively massive skill ceiling. The main gamemodes all feel different and are all a blast (if you think of CTF as unlimited deathmatch lol). The artstyle is timeless! This game understands that burst damage is the most fun part of any shooter!

I wish I could go on, but anyone reading knows why this is a negative review. Valve's inaction on the bot issue is unacceptable on its own, but the absolute radio silence for YEARS (one damage control tweet that amounted to nothing doesn't count) about the ordeal and about TF2's future in general is downright pathetic for any developer, let alone Valve to be trying to pull. This is an unprecedented level of game neglect unheard of in the industry for an issue that is stopping the game from being playable right now. The only way me, or you, or anyone else in the world can play this game right now is by finding a community server likely owned by penny pinchers that want to throw ads in your face or is otherwise horribly managed. The few well-maintained servers out there are played by people at a skill level that is frankly well beyond the reach of anyone that hasn't already dumped a good couple hundred hours into honing their skill. I've never been a serious player, but even still, with 1,8k hours I can just barely keep up in an Uncletopia server. This problem isn't anyone's fault but Valve's, really. The massive range of low-average skill levels has no place anymore now that Valve servers are mostly unplayable, which is just really tragic to see. I still have fun in Uncletopia / other "sweaty-semi-casual" servers, but essentially anyone close to or below that certain skill level is going to have a tough time in these servers and likely be dogged on for dragging the team down. Meanwhile, if you want to play a Valve server where the skill disparity is a lot less intense, have fun spending 10 minutes or so queuing up for a good 2fort server that isn't infested with bots and playing endless deathmatch, which is admittedly fun but only contains a fraction of the gameplay depth TF2 has to offer, with much less emphasis on the "team" part that really makes the other gamemodes click.

I could rant more, but I feel like I've gotten enough of the point across. If Valve proves me and the rest of the community wrong and shows they can care enough to make some serious fixes, I'll dump these last hours and write that sappy review about how much I love this game.
If not, this might be where it ends for me and this game. Those years before the bot crisis really kicked off were some of the most fun I've ever had.
It's such a shame.

Valve has always done this thing where they don't say a word about anything because it's easier than communicating with your playerbase and then having that playerbase hold you to your word or expect you to do something. Technically they COULD be doing something, there could be a whole team working on it and trying to figure out how to fix the game, but in reality that's nothing more than wishful thinking. We only know that there's like 1 guy doing barebones maintenance on this game, and bless that person honestly.

However, it just doesn't make any sense. You can ignore any sort of emotional appeal to TF2's legacy, community, importance for the industry or Valve, anything subjective and sentimental? You can wipe that out and it still wouldn't make sense because even if you ignore that, it's still a massive game that makes Valve a truckload of money. 

You'd think it would be in their interest to ensure that the game is in a healthy and appealing state. Not just to avoid bleeding players or attracting new ones (which obviously feeds into trading and their income), but for their own image. You think people would be paying clown prices for a garrish hat with even more hideous special effects if TF2 had 1k players? Obviously not. The same way, investing into a game that might just get abandoned and overrun by cheaters doesn't seem too appealing.

I despise the skin market that Valve created, so it's annoying to make arguments based on it, but it certainly seems like Valve would care more about money than anything else. It seems clear that there's no artistic drive to support something you've created, and there's clearly no sense of responsibility to at least maintain it in a proper state for the sake of hundreds of thousands of people who love TF2.

It really pains me to say it but ... I believe Team Fortress 2 is dead.

Trying to add a matchmaking/quickplay system has only harmed this game then it has [i]ever helped it[/i], even before casual, back to the time when quickplay was added, there were reports of community servers struggling to properly fill up there player slots, alongside complaints of being shoved into servers filled with valve bots, or servers with virus ridden MOTDs, quickplay had many many flaws, but community servers still had thrived. 

But by the time casual was added? So many community servers now were not only struggling, but had straight up died to the point where only a few had remained and were constantly full cause no one had anywhere else to go. The bot crises I'd argue [i]is[/i], in fact, a direct result of the casual matchmaking system allowing bot hosters to fill party queues with them, (it only takes 4 full parties to fill a valve server btw). This, in addition to disallowing ad-hoc and votekicking on valve official servers, has created an incredibly exploitative and abusable system that makes trying to play on official servers feel like pulling teeth, this isn't sustainable, and since valve servers lack proper moderation or community created anti-cheats, there is no longer a possible way of managing this.

Where does that leave us? While I can't say in good faith that valve should just remove casual outright (even though thats what id think is best), I do think it's become clear that the way it is designed has always been extremely flawed, and that community servers, due to the fundamental way they're managed by real people, do not suffer these horrendous list of issues. I think valve, rather then trying to fix the casual system and all the complication that entails, should instead look to the community and support the servers within the server browser that are still keeping the game truly alive. I think a good start to this would be updating the UI of the server browser which hasn't changed since 2007. In the browsers current state, it is extremely archaic and unintuitive for newer players who'd sooner use the casual search tool due to its simpler nature. We think both giving it a fresh, more accessible look and encouraging its use over casual is a good first step in the right direction. After bolstering the server browser, valve could potentially work closer with the community and what the larger tf2 community to take notes to improve both their own servers along with ours. 

In summary, I think community servers have been the lifeblood of this game ever since release, and I think valve could help this game a lot more by contributing to and bolstering those communities rather then fixing a flawed server system that people have been complaining about ever since meet your match happened, Whether valve fixes their servers or not, the future of this game has and always will be the communities that people create within it.

[i][b]UPDATE[/b] 7/10/2024:[/i] There have been a number of accounts asserting that the majority of the bots in this game have been banned, and official servers are largely clean now. This is great. It's delightful to see the pathetic bot hosters receive the hammer, squirming in their chairs and [i]hopefully[/i] questioning their life choices. Nonetheless, if you still care about this game, don't say "thanks", only say "good job". As long as the official game and inventory servers continue to run, they require maintenance, and I affirm this obvious fact with personal experience running my own web and mail servers. Do not buy from Mann Co. or any of Valve's other in-game microtransaction stores, primarily because it is important to keep the pressure on (and they are a large reason why the game was so botted to begin with). Persist, and surely you will see to it that one day you get your game back.

Team Fortress 2 was a favorite pasttime for an entire generation getting home from school every weekday. Unlike the more competitive multiplayer games, it never demanded too much from the player like it was some lifelong commitment to tie one's self up in. Even if you had never played this game back then, you may have seen the iconic nine classes appear in countless Garry's Mod and SFM skits over the years. The fact that the characters here have achieved such a level of ubiquity without the need for billion dollar marketing is a display of how brilliant the art direction was.

Certainly, this was one of the first games which convinced me of the merits of the first person shooter, and one of the first which got me into Steam to begin with. I've poured several hundred hours in here screwing around in various servers and generally having a good time. That was up until 2016... in my specific case, it had more to do with my interests shifting, but I did touch it exactly once more in 2018, well after that notorious failure of an update which tried to pull TF2 away from its roots and into more of a competitive game on the level of Counter-Strike and Dota. I wasn't pleased with how it seemed to become sterilized in such a manner. So, I turned away, uninstalled the game, cashed out my measly inventory a few years later, and never looked back, not feeling much from it...

So then, why now am I writing about this game? If you're not already aware, the official servers for Team Fortress 2 have been neglected to such an egregious extent for the past five years that even I cannot simply tune it out, having formerly been a rigorous player. These servers are heavily infested with bots which are intently designed to render the game unplayable. They're aimbotting, impersonating real users, spamming vile rhetoric, kicking players out, and largely eluding Valve's anti-cheat system all the way through. That's only scratching the surface; if you look it up yourself, you'll see it gets a whole lot worse.

What has Valve done about this? Nothing much, really. Actually, in recent times since the #SaveTF2 movement, they've done worse than nothing. Not only have they made no recent effort whatsoever to combat the bots, they now have the nerve to introduce new microtransaction products to TF2's store as they neglect the game. So, it's gone from apathy or laziness to pure spite.

Yes, I know. You can play in the community servers, which are much more proactive in keeping the bots out, often using freely available modules to aid in the process. But for the average person who doesn't look too much into things, they won't think this is a thing. The official servers effectively represent the game, and if they're unusable, so is the entire game for them.

For a multi-billion dollar corporation, this is pathetic. I had a lot of faith in Valve before, because they held onto some form of a "don't be evil" philosophy for a long time. I've made tons of excuses to myself that there was some good cause to some of their more questionable practices, like maybe the so-called "Mann-Conomy" was a tip jar so that one day we'd get an incredible new game from them. Oh, dear...

Recent leaks suggest Valve is planning to release a new game which is apparently a confusing salad of already established ideas from completely different games. It looks generic, but that's not what I intend to highlight here. With TF2 becoming a completely unsafe environment, and even Counter-Strike 2 suffering similar neglect, how can anyone be expected to have confidence in such a new game? At the rate things are going, it's bound to be dead on arrival.

You can invalidate me all you want with how I haven't touched the game in years, but Team Fortress 2 MATTERED to thousands of people. It brought everyone together and formed many friendships, and supplemented the creativity of some of the brightest animators on the internet. It was able to do all of this on such a large scale because it was such a well designed and fully operational game which Valve used to vigilantly upkeep for the lot of a decade.

Some of you might have become aware of the #StopKillingGames movement following the shutdown of The Crew, which involved shutting down the servers and rendering the game completely unplayable with no recourse. It's effectively robbery, but as we see here, there happens to be more than one way to kill a game. A new generation's perception of Team Fortress 2 is forever tainted because of Valve's complete refusal to tackle the bot crisis head on, and these players will never get to experience the joys we had to the fullest.

I can no longer look at this company in a positive light. I guess I should've seen it coming; Valve is not really a game company anymore. Its primary focus is more so digital logistics than anything else, transporting other developers' games to people's computers. It does that job well, but that's about all I can say anymore. Your dreams of a Half-Life 3 release are down the drain, and you're gonna have to accept that this is the new reality of the company. It will take a long time to sink in, but the truth will give you new life.

Point being, you should play G-Darius HD.

167063646.review:
I played this like, twice, before COVID. All I remember is getting destroyed and beating someone in 1v1s as medic until they got pissed and said the bone saw was OP. 

During COVID, however,
My extra free time led me to try anything I could think of, eventually settling on TF2. It wasn't for the gameplay. It wasn't for the memes. It was for the community. It was for conga-ing into sticky traps and watching the demo responsible crumple to the floor rather than kill me. It was for the people who stopped fighting just to help me learn airblast deflect timings. It was for the scouts who'd mercilessly batter themselves to build my uber. It was for the spies who warned me about upcoming sentries. It was for all the times I returned the favor.
I was hooked on the joy of bonding with people by crouching and aggressively swinging my head around.
I was enamored by the people giving out free gear to new players.
I was charmed by the goofy, syrupy sweet global announcements when someone gifted a wedding ring

Of course, that's not the full story. I've been preached at by evangelicals and told I'll burn in hell. I've been called slurs I never knew existed. I've been kicked for being trans. I've received scam offers and fishy links. But, honestly though, that's been such a small part of my experience.

I was warned that TF2 was a cesspit of a community. That's simply not true. Without omniscient or automated moderation like in many social media or games currently seen, there is a lot of dirt that's visible. But it's just as much dirt as anywhere else in reality. And without cleaning out the dirt, you also see just how clean the rest is. Teams vote to remote bigoted members. People stick up for each other in chat. And every once in a blue moon, someone has the patience to really talk to one of those edgelords and give them an opportunity to change their behavior for the better.

When the bots struck, it took a long time for people to adapt. Users who never knew votekicks were a thing had to learn how to do it quickly to stop a team from being overrun. Players became hypervigilant against snipers and spammers. There are few things as disheartening as watching someone give up on having fun the way they looked forward to all day.

Now it seems the bots are here to stay. Despite incredible teamwork and initiative, the inflow of joining players just become too dense with bots to allow any fun even if the server itself is kept mostly clean. This game is probably not worth the time money or effort to fix to a lot of people. But to me, and to the other people leaving reviews and begging Valve, it really truly is. 

When you read this, and the rest of this sea of reviews, don't forget that these aren't nameless, faceless automata like what we're fighting against. Each and every review comes from someone who cares about the community. Each and every review comes from someone who acts as a spycrab to make people laugh, who swaps to scout to build uber and engi to build teleporters, someone who gives away gear to new players, someone who stands up for fellow players. Each and Every review comes from someone who's life has been changed by this game and wants to watch it change more lives.

I have nearly 1000 hours in this game. I want to pass that threshold in a bot-free world.
No, I would not recommend you play this game. Yes, I would recommend you fight for its right to exist.


EDIT I have passed 1000 hours in a bot free game. It's been clean, peaceful, and wonderful to reconnect. I will, however, leave this review standing as-is as another mark of what happened and what has changed in this game. In case bots return or a new threat looms

A game doesn't need grade A realistic graphics to be fun, all it needs is a flustering soul behind it. TF2 is different from all the other shooter games out there; it has charm behind its characters, its maps, and its guns. Who wants just another generic modern soldier with an AK-47? I want my funny black scottish cyclops holding a sword and a shield to decapitate his enemies! The real reason I love this game however, comes down to not just the gameplay, the intricacies of the characters, the hilariousness of what an come out of a match, but it is for the community that surrounds this game. Uncle Dane, Solarlight, Jontohil2, and Great Blue are just a small fraction of the youtubers who make the content that makes this game so incredible. And not to undermine the short films Valve has created themselves with the Meet the Team videos, canonically fleshing out the characters we already know and love, along with an entire comic book series about them as well that was just recently finished this year too.

2024 has been an amazing year for Team Fortress 2 fans, with them finally eradicating the bots that have plagued the game for six years, but Valve continuing to keep the bots away and completing TF2's story once and for all. It is ultimately okay if we don't get an update, just as long as Valve can do just enough to keep this game working for the millions of fans of it out there. Thank you Valve, for this masterpiece.

166813799.review:
Usually I disapprove of review bombing in response to the developer's actions (or rather inaction in this case) as it often discourages people from playing an amazing game because of some drama they may not necessarily care about.

This is not the case here.

Are people review bombing this game because they are unhappy with Valve? Yes.

Is every single one of those reviews justified? Absolutely.

Looking at the state of the game now, I cannot, in good faith, recommend it to anyone. Casual is just overflowing with bots and it's never the question of "if" you're going to see them whenever you play, it's "when".

In the best case scenario, your match will be regularly disrupted by a bot that will hopefully be kicked but is still incredibly annoying even if it's just one.

In the worst case scenario, the amount of bots will outnumber the players and you will be kicked out by them instead.

This is incredibly sad to see as TF2 is definetly one of the most unique first person shooters out there that's brimming with personality and is incredibly fun to play but for now I can't recommend playing it, at least not untill Valve does something to address the bot issue permanently.

Team Fortress 2 is an undying gem. A whole generation of people was born during this game's relevancy in internet culture, and it's for a good reason: Everything. Just. Ticks. Right. This game came from an era when Marvel one-liners weren't a Pony's One Trick of all media, when Free to Play didn't necessarily mean "Unenjoyable for less than 30$\mo", when game development was a form of art. And now it has been gathering dust for years due to negligence on the Valve's side.

AN UPDATE! I had to rewrite a detailed part of this review, since a lot of things had changed recently. But in my eyes, the point still stands clear.

So, what's wrong with TF2 now? Well, the main issue, being the overwhelming amount of malicious actors abusing the game and its community for years, seems to be fixed, partially, for now. Not sure for how long this is going to stay, and I'm not ready to let go of the fact that it took years for the ban wave to arrive. As for now, I guess that the best time to play the game is now, so break a leg!
I am still not recommending this game. The reason behind it is that the game is still being treated like it was after the Jungle Inferno update - a seasonal money furnace. More community made stuff bloats current item pool even more (BOTLER 2000 follower?? Absolutely not!), new maps stretching the playerbase even thinner, and the community server tab is still as unreadable for new players as ever, discouraging people from creating and playing said servers. Most of the official content has already been made it seems like, unless you're into gambling, and it would be fine if the content we do have weren't constantly distilled with whimsical shinies. I'm not saying that community made content is bad though, it's great, and fun as its own thing! It's just that this being alongside everything that is official kind of makes the "official" side of TF2 less directed. I do not support handicapping user experience for the sake of milking more money.

UPDATE OVER!

With that said, I encourage readers to spread the word about Valve's negligence towards its client base, and adwise them to not support this behaviour financially. By buying games from steam, spending money on microtransactions, even participating in Steam Community Market, you are supporting Valve's malicious business practices.

VALVE'S GAMES AND YOUR STEAM ACCOUNT ARE NOT A GOOD INVESTMENT!

TF2 NEEDS TO BE FIXED!

I've been a player for a long time and I absolutely love this game, the class dynamics, the weapon choices, the maps, hell, even getting pubstomped by the MLG Spy with the Kunai + DR combo or the Soldier with a Medic glued to his ass can be fun and a learning experience.

1. The games have amazing atmospheres.
2. They have creative fantasy worlds with a mix of steam punk, urban landscapes, magic, medieval stuff, etc. 
3. The stealth mechanics are satisfying and great. Going around different places, knocking out guards, picking doors, using water arrows to take out torches, and stealing loot that is used to buy gear for the next level. It is great.
4. The cutscenes are beautiful and well voice acted.

To be fair, in the first game, some levels are in non-urban/natural environments which makes them more of a slog. However, the series grew out of this problem in the following games.

EDIT (08/02/24): After seeing the work put in to ban the aimbots and provide a summer update with quality maps, I'm willing to change my review to a positive one. I'm glad to see that TF2 is once again "the most fun you can have online". I hope that the devs continue to provide support to keep that statement true.

Original Review (06/04/24):

This is the game I have the most hours in across all games on every platform. It truly was a timeless masterpiece I kept going back to due to its fun gameplay and unique community. I say "was" because unfortunately, Valve is neglecting the game to the point where aimbots have completely taken over TF2's casual servers for nearly 5 years, making it unplayable. While community servers remain bot-free and keep the community intact, it's hard to recommend this game to newer players whose first experience would be joining a casual server, getting their ears blasted by bots spamming in voice chat, seeing racist, homophobic, and/or transphobic messages in text chat, and getting killed instantly by an aimbot.

Amidst all of this, Valve has done nearly nothing to fix the issue. Occasionally, an update comes out that breaks all the bots, but that's only temporarily, as they come back within the next day or two. About two years ago, Valve made a tweet saying that they hear us and are attempting to fix the issue. Ever since then, there's been radio silence. And yet, Valve continues to monetize this game by pushing cosmetic items and loot boxes. The whole topic of loot boxes is an entirely different topic, but I would have no issue with them doing this if the game wasn't in the sad state that it's in. The fact that Valve is still profiting off an unplayable game is shameful, and I expect better from them with the legacy they have.

Currently, I cannot recommend this game to anyone with all the aimbots overrunning casual servers. It's quite literally in an unplayable state. Should Valve commit to the promise they made two years ago and fix the botting issue, I will happily change my review to a positive one. As it stands right now though, I'm hurt to see such a legendary game in the first person shooter genre fall into the state that it's in. Do better Valve, fix TF2.

166676342.review:
TF2 is a Masterpiece. It is a genre defining title that didn't just pave the way for team-based shooters, but was a defining moment in gaming history for the PC as a platform. It is a 17 year old title that has withstood the test of time to continue being one of the single most popular titles in modern day, even after 2 decades and over half a decade with no substantial updates. For all these reasons, I would recommend TF2, for its community, its genuinely enjoyable and chaotic gameplay, and for the simple fact that of all games from that age, it alone stands tall over even newer games today.

But I cannot. For the last half a decade, TF2 has been in an increasingly poor state due to the raging issue of bots. This isn't a typical issue where you'll see a few bots in a game, this is an issue where the vast majority of players in a server may just be bots. You will be killed by snipers spinning while aiming straight up, you will be kicked by bots voting out random players, you will not ab able to enjoy this game for any period of time on the official matchmaking servers. TF2 is not a healthy game. It has been tormented by the bot crisis for years, all with the illusion of the game being in a healthy state due to its inflated numbers from the number of bots. It's been estimated (with reasearch into botted accounts) that more than 2/3rds of the active players on TF2 at any given time are, in fact, bots.

TF2 is a piece of gaming history. This piece of history is being ruined by a company that refuses to take any actions towards actually fixing the issue TF2 has been suffering through. The last acknowledgement of TF2's issues was in a twitter post in 2022 that ultimately resulted in nothing. TF2 certainly isn't dying, but it's nowhere near healthy. If the bot pandemic continues, it will gradually whittle away at what remains of the real playerbase until the game becomes nothing more but a bunch of bot infested servers, filled with idlers that are farming item crates for money. Obviously, nobody wants that.

I am overjoyed about this fact. Go play this game, best game of all time, etc.. If the bots return I won´t hesitate to change this review again ... Valve ( ͡ಠ ʖ̯ ͡ಠ). (Bye bye all the people that gave the negative review a thumps up, since the recommendation changes they all get deleted)

This is my favourite game of all time. Even if it's old, the gameplay is still one of the best experiences I ever had in gaming. I played the Overwatchs, Valorants and The Finals of this world and enjoyed them. But nothing hits as many marks as this game. Sadly, casual mode has been flooded with hacking bots for years now, making it close to impossible to play an evening with you and your buddies without encountering a load of them on every server you get matched on. 

This can go the following ways:
- There are a few bots on the server. Which, after coordinating with your team get votekicked out. Everyone is happy, team 
   numbers are now unbalanced until autobalance decides to do something about it. You can play the game for up to half an 
   hour untill the next bots join the server, repeating the cycle.
- The server you're joining, or the one you cleansed half an hour ago, gets filled with bots that due to their amount or lack 
  of teamcoordination cant be votekicked. Leading to either the bots kicking you from the server, forcing a requeue or you 
  giving up on the server and requeuing yourself willingly.
- The server you get into is a happy place without any bots on which you can play until we cycle back to the first and 
  second point mentioned.

Over the years I had a lot of fun here, played casual, played competitive, participated in the trading community, joined silly community servers, found some of my now closest friends, even a relationship at some point. I have a thousand good memories that I would not want to miss. Now I can't recommend anyone I know to play the game with me. I used to bring people to play with me from other areas of my life and they had a blast. I can't do that nowadays because of the frustrating cycle mentioned above. The game's gameplay and the people in it used to speak for themselves in showing its appeal.

If you read a bit into the bot problem, you start to realize the almost mafia-like structures that seemed to have been built around it and the levels of harassment anyone speaking out against these issues has to face. From doxxing to swatting, everything is possible. You just start to wonder how the hell this could have happened in any way, shape or form.

My biggest hope would be that Valve gets to fix all of this and that I, some months down the line, can add an edit note to this review that says :"Everything is fine again, lol", but I can't do that for now. The last time I heard a Valve employee mention the bot crisis casually, they talked about not doing anything about it.

I haven't bought anything from either the in-game store or the community market related to TF2 items in a while, maybe that could help ... I dont know to be honest. Here is me hoping Valve cares about a revenue stream getting smaller. Even if it's grasping at straws. If I managed to convince one person to join me in that protest, this review was worth it.

Overall, I'm just sad. I used to love this game. If I think about TF2 nowadays, I think back to all the great times I had with it ... and then mentally add: “A shame what happened to it.”

What's left for me from this game? It's either something like TF2Classic, which isn't too hard to set up but not as convenient as clicking install on Steam, leaving a few friends out already. Or joining community servers with playerbases that have a different kind of mindset than the casual experience I'm so fond of.

As a closing statement, I'm going to quote FUNKe from a video he made around 2–3 years ago: 
“I love TF2, and I miss it.”

I've played Team Fortress 2 since 2012, and it's probably my favorite game of all time. It has amazing mechanical depth, and has tremendous staying power. An average active playerbase of around 30,000 players (discounting Idle bots and trade bots that run the game all hours) is really good for a game this old.

Which is why the cheaterbots are such a frustrating problem! Do you have any idea how discouraging that is for newbies?

It is rare to see any game, let alone a multiplayer pvp game, have active players for over a decade. It is even more rare for that game to have people making new art, discussions, and new items to be used in that game, and TF2 has both in spades.

And yet, if I want to *play* this amazing game? I'm lucky if I can get into a casual match with people after 10 minutes of queueing and re-queueing from all the bots.

Please Valve, put down your shiny new toys like the Steam Deck and Deadlock for a few weeks and have some folks work on an anti-cheat or SOMETHING. Counter Strike 2 has a similar issue with cheaters and could also heavily benefit, as could your new projects!

Reviews are for new players deciding if they want to choose an exciting new game to spend their time on. What then is the new player experience for TF2 in the year 2024? 

You, Bright Eyed New Player, hits the Casual browser and queues into a random Valve-run server. The first experience you are likely to get as soon as you load into a game, even prior to seeing the class select screen? Some bot spamming obnoxious profanities into your ears at max volume. You are then immediately kicked before understanding what is happening.

 A slightly more generous take on what could be your experience, prospective New Player. You choose a class (Lets be real, probably Scout), walk out of spawn, and are immediately headshot by the legion of spinning hackers on the enemy team. You search for the keybind to ask you team what happened only to be greeted by this message "voice/text chat is not allowed on this account". A quick search online tells you that you cannot communicate in any way unless you pay Valve money. Ostensibly this is to counter bots, though you will likely have already encountered many bots spamming racism and hate into the chat and into your ears. You are then promptly kicked from the server. 

So you finally get a server where you aren't immediately kicked in under 10 seconds by spinning bots shouting profanities and actually get to play a round of TF2. Except you are still headshot immediately by a sniper within half a second of leaving spawn. But this cannot be a bot, no, they have hats and are proclaiming in chat that they are human. They even have a couple friends backing them up, so they must certainly just be incredible at the game and using some item to see you through walls and while invisible. You then proceed to have "The most fun you can have online" and are stuck in spawn by a hacker for the whole round with nary a chance of pushing out. 

By all means, if this seems fun for you download the game.
Roll the dice to see which of the above options will be your experience.
Maybe you get astoundingly lucky and get a server that can deal with bots after a few minutes and can play a somewhat normal round.
Its unlikely, but possible.
Maybe you search online and find a server that Valve does not run that is free from bots, queue for a year waiting for a spot to join and immediately get stomped by people with literal thousands of hours of experience. 
This is considered the "Good" option by many players.

This used to be "The Most Fun You Can Have Online" some years ago, but now the game is something you must struggle against to have fun. Truly, I have no idea how a new player is supposed to experience TF2 as it was in the glory days.

166637736.review:
Christmas Day 2010. After a day of opening presents, late into the night, I open up my laptop next to my older brother and he pulls up this very page, and inputs his credit card details to pay the $20 to buy me this game. This was all I wanted when I was 12. I thought about this game so much it consumed me, and that one generous purchase gave me 13 and a half years of pure joy. I have played or thought about this game for a majority of my lifetime. It is still in my Top 5 favorite of all time.

And it's not just me. This game is a cultural touchstone. Every single one of these characters has been recognized or at least noticed not only by people who have never played TF2, but by people who don't play video games. Their feature in SFM shorts has influenced film making. Its class-based team shooter formula has been copied by titles far more successful than it is today- titles that Valve is now borrowing game elements from. Its characters are a textbook example in visual design. And all of that still isn't enough for Valve to consider giving the game some tender love and care.

And what puzzles me most about this lack of investment is that it seems to be unjustifiable in terms of a business perspective. With this loyal of a fanbase spending regular amounts of money on in-game purchases, and this much of an outcry over the state of a beloved cultural icon, I would only assume that a legitimate update on this game, that would not only fix the bots but also add new content, would get its investment back within minutes of its release, and generate tons of revenue. And we aren't even asking for an update. We're just asking for a fix to the bots, so that we can go back to the game that has defined so many of our lives.

I hope Deadlock succeeds. I genuinely do. Because if it fails, I can only think of one reason why it would- neglect. Valve as a company seems to be infallible in the eyes of its fans. That Photoshop of Gabe Newell as Jesus is so ubiquitous I have no idea what the original looks like. But if Deadlock is going to function as a game, it's going to need a different anti-cheat than VAC. And if Deadlock can use something other than VAC, so can TF2, I can only assume. Maybe that's not the solution. Maybe it's much more complex than that, but Deadlock will face the same challenges TF2 does, and I genuinely believe that fixing TF2 would not come at the cost of their current project. If it would, I would really love to know why. 

This review is rambly now, and I hate editing, so I'll end here. To call TF2 a great game doesn't even make sense. This is one of the most influential pieces of media in the past two decades. And I'm about to uninstall it.

I owe it to this game for the many friends I've found and stayed in touch with for years and over a decade now, but I cannot in good conscience recommend this game in its current state. 

Public server matchmaking, one of the "latest" major features added to it, has been infested with bot accounts that ruin this experience for any casual player, whether through blatant aimbot hacks, chat spam, mic spam, by ejecting you out of a match with votekicks, or by everything of what was mentioned above.

Valve have been neglecting the severity of this issue for years, despite still frequently adding cosmetic items to their in-game store, thus profiting from the game as a product. And even though community servers are still there, available in the server browser like they have been long before matchmaking was implemented, I do not want to spend my time looking for such server, just to have a quick 30-minute quick match to entertain myself. Not to mention any of the potential issues that could come from community servers in forms of gigabytes of content being required to download at awfully low speed, dealing with community elitism or moderators with superiority complex, or abundance of confusing plugins filling the screen. But this isn't about community servers right now, I just wanted to quickly get into a game, and start playing, just like the game offers me to do in their own main menu.

Team Fortress 2 was what could have been considered a classic for its genre, and the matchmaking, while not perfect in practice (team imbalances etc), was still enough to scratch the itch for a quick fun game with people of varying skill degrees and backgrounds. Sure, Valve doesn't owe me or anybody else their time to deal with this problem (although highly debatable, since people are still buying and trading items on the regular, including the marketplace), there is a massive playerbase who's been begging, pleading for them to [u][b]permanently[/b][/u] deal with the ongoing bot crisis in their beloved game.

[i]"TF2 community, we hear you! We love this game and know you do, too. We see how large this issue has become and are working to improve things."[/i]

[url=https://x.com/TeamFortress/status/1529970640224018433]Valve said this in their official TF2 Twitter statement on May 27, 2022.[/url] It has been two years since then, and whatever they've done has only temporarily stifled bot activity, for a very short time. 

Dedicated fans will know that Valve are not a company of many words, but if those are going to be their last words towards the public plea to take action against what could be considered a rampantly increasing artificial plague within their own product, then I have no other option but to leave a negative recommendation and move on.

ORIGINAL REVIEW TEXT:

  TF2 is a classic FPS that endures only due to its passionate fanbase. The characters are still iconic, the gameplay at its best is still fun with a ton of mechanical variety. You can have hour-long games with tense back and forths finally ending in a climactic finish, and you can have silly experiences just hanging around with friends or strangers. You can still have a fun time if you are a longtime veteran of the game, but I cannot recommend it to new players due to the neglect from the developers of the game, Valve. The game is flooded with cheaters, both human and robot. A new player to the game not only needs to learn the actual game mechanics, but also about bots. Things like, "what does a bot name look like?" and "when should you re-queue because a server is unrecoverable and completely lost to bots?" If a new player didn't spend money on the game (a free to play or "F2P"),  they cannot even ASK these questions, because in the last few years Valve disabled chat usage for F2P players.

  The F2P chat ban has not solved the issue of the bots spamming the chat because bot hosters just buy premium for the bots. It's not that expensive for them since it takes months for the bots to be banned, if they even get banned. Instead, it has ruined the experience for new players. New players can't ask about their weapons. They can't chat along with everyone else. They can't even use the hotkey bound by default by the game to call for a medic. Given that the game is a [b]team[/b] game the chat ban has a direct negative effect on the gameplay for the F2P player and their team. Valve could theoretically revert the F2P chat ban at any time just as quickly as they started it. Valve should know by now the chat ban has done nothing to stop bots from spamming the chat, but it remains in place. Is Valve that desperate for bot hoster's money?

  Even with all of these issues, Valve cannot even be bothered to state anything about the game beyond the fact that basically no one is working on the game, nor interested in working on it. Valve claims to want to avoid "treadmill work" where recurring maintenance is needed, but is perfectly fine with the "treadmill work" of releasing new content for people to pay for. More microtransaction crates are added to the game while the game on official Valve servers remains pretty much unplayable if you don't know how to properly navigate those servers in the modern era of TF2. While TF2 may not make anywhere near as much money as Counterstrike, I would assume that it makes enough money to hire a contractor to manually ban obvious cheating spinbots if nothing else.

  While the game isn't dead due to the community who has stuck with it for over a decade, the game [i]will[/i] slowly wither away unless Valve takes action against bots and cheaters, and allows the F2P players to have a voice again. All of which seems very unlikely.

  For anyone who does want to try start playing as a new player regardless, I recommend either avoiding casual or actively taking the time to learn about the bot issue first:
- Look for snipers with robotic non-human movement, huge aim snaps, or aiming straight up 100% of the time to identify bots. Some bots do not play sniper but may still aim straight up or have huge aim snaps.
- Leave servers when one team is 50% full of bots or more.
- Avoid healing bots. Don't push forward when bots are present to be courteous to the enemy team.
- Always kick bots as soon as possible because bots will begin votekicks on real players when they can.
- When a votekick starts, do not vote to kick unless you are sure that the team overwhelmingly believes the player in question to be a bot, or even better, verify the player is actually a bot yourself.
- Keep an eye on the chat to see if anyone is calling out bots on either team. People aren't always correct or truthful, but it does mean you should check on the player in question.
- Avoid certain maps/gamemodes during bot waves (the CTF gamemode and the map Harvest get especially bad).

  As for community servers, "Uncletopia" servers exist but they are not the same as the "true" casual experience that Valve intended. There are class limits and the players tend to be more skilled and more focused on playing the game to win, which is not a bad thing but may not interest all players."Skial" servers are closer to the "vanilla TF2" experience but most of their servers are 24/7 servers for specific maps with only a couple true casual servers. Other "vanilla TF2" casual servers exist but are often empty.

  Although this review may be posted at the same time as many other negative reviews, this review is sincere. I cannot recommend the game to new players anymore.

For whatever it's worth, Valve, fix TF2.

I’ve been playing TF2 since launch, and I love the community. More than a decade later, folks are pushing the engine to do things that Valve never thought possible. Even if we ignore the fact that Valve frequently fails to compile these maps correctly for events, there is so much innovation and passion in this community. But unfortunately, Valve has not invested in reasonable anti-cheat mitigations. Most of the online users are cheating griefing aimbots or idle bots that manipulate the economy. Volunteers have already identified tens of thousands of these bots with public information. Valve could do a more sophisticated analysis themselves. But they don’t. They could work with the community to allow us to moderate. But they don’t. They could open source the game and leave it in control of a community operated foundation, who can implement cheat mitigations on casual servers. But they don’t. But guess what - they’ll happily take your money, even though the game is unplayable most of the time. They’ll invest in new games which inherit the same flaws and immediately get plagued with the same problems. And then they’ll move on, upset at the negative response.

This game, more so than almost all other Valve games, is such an important piece of history and the cultural zeitgeist. You’ll find no other game which three generations of people know and fondly remember from their childhood and wish they could play today without dealing with the bot problem.

This makes me sad. There is truly nothing like TF2, and there never will be again if platforms don’t invest into moderation tools to fix this problem. I’m also certain that the community has engineers who would join Valve to further this mission - if Valve is interested.

I hope that Valve realizes that there are so many different ways they can #FixTF2 and also make newer games remain viable.

166617551.review:
Team Fortress 2 is a one of a kind game. While many games have progressed to a point where TF2 can feel old, TF2 still has its own special feel to it. While many point out how other games have abilities, cooldowns, and ults. I think pointing these out wouldn't fully describe it. TF2 is built off of older design for video games. Before they wanted to simplify things for a wider audience. I'm not saying this is bad, but it's just something TF2 has unique to it in the genre. Yet it still remains easy to get into and hard to master. Often harder to master a single class than it would take to master several in other games. Yet there's still simple classes like Pyro, Heavy and Soldier. Realistically anyone can pick up these classes and get use out of them. Even if they don't tap into their full potential. (Looking at you, Soldier.)

But all of the good aspects of TF2 don't matter when the game is littered with bots. While community servers like Uncletopia lack bots, their players are too skilled or experienced for newcomers. Not to say that anyone who goes on Uncletopia should feel bad. There should be a place for more serious games of TF2. But TF2 currently lacks a truly good casual experience unless its an instant respawn server that runs 24/7 on 2fort.

This is ultimately why I don't recommend newcomers to currently play TF2. Casual is swarmed with bots, making a learning experience difficult to achieve. While most places free of bots are often sweaty or just slop content that won't provide a true experience that reflects the game. If bots were to ever be removed, I'd say TF2 should be played. As a shining example of how older FPS games like Quake used to be designed. Sadly, this just can't be the case with Valve's neglect.

166606569.review:
I first downloaded this game in 2013 and, despite dropping off a couple times over the years, it has been a reliably fun game for that entire time. That was until 2020, when a group of degenerate trolls became capable of hosting large numbers of bots that do something very simple: They join Valve servers, pick sniper, and aimbot everything that isn't them. This practice allows these people to shut down dozens of servers simultaneously without even being present at their computers. As a result, it has become largely impossible to play the game without entering community servers, which aren't a proper replacement due to the work required to find a decent community server that can facilitate casual play.

This game has been my go to for many years precisely because new games don't do what this game does. Modern shooters are all focused on one thing: competitive play. The problem is that forced competitive play is bound to turn into a toxic shit flinging fest where everyone hates everyone else including themselves because trying to get 5 other random people to work together is near impossible. The developers of Team Fortress 2 figured this out before even making this game and it's one of the large reasons it has stood the test of time. Even with all the bots and lack of support from Valve this game is simply irreplaceable to me. Other games keep trying and failing to do what TF2 does and it's so frustrating to see this wonderful game fall victim to an awful combination of developer apathy and degenerate jerks trying to ruin it and stop anyone that wants to simply play the game as Valve intended.

I am saying this now because enough is enough. I'm going to continue playing this game but I will not be giving another cent to Valve through this game until they have done what needs to be done to fix these problems and introduce a more permanent solution to the problem. Sure that may sound counter intuitive to keep playing this game but it's not playing the game that keeps the servers alive, at least not just playing. Servers cost money, and without the stream of income from players like me those servers cannot survive. I also won't recommend anyone new play this game for the same reason.

There's also another reason Valve needs to get on this problem: It's not just TF2 anymore, because Counter Strike 2 runs on the source engine (granted it's source 2 rather than source 1), this means that Counter Strike 2 is vulnerable to the same botting problem that TF2 has been subject to for years now. If Valve doesn't take action to fix this, it WILL spill out into their biggest game, and then they'll be forced to act in a way that TF2's community simply can't force.

The ball is in your court Valve, either fix this, or it's going to get worse, it will bring in Counter Strike 2's community, which carries far more weight, and that will be a problem they can't ignore.

EDIT: So it seems they hired a contractor to actually fix the problem. Well I guess I can go back to recommending this game. Better late than never, but time will tell if the bots truly stay away.
